A camera bolted to a ceiling. Very wide and barrel-distorted, crushed nearly to grey, grainy, levelled and stabilised because nobody is holding it — and stamped with the time.

Fires a real light on the frame you take, so faces near the camera come out hot and the far side of the room falls away. It has to charge between shots. Other players see the photo, not the pop.

Out of film — reload to keep shooting
How big the grain is. This is what separates film from digital noise: a fast negative enlarged from a small frame has grain you can pick out, while a sensor turned up produces a much finer speckle.
A fine speckle, the way a video sensor at high gain looks.
The middle of the range — a slow film, or an instant print's dye texture.
Grain you can count, the way a fast consumer negative comes back from a machine scan.
The heaviest texture there is, for a small sensor pushed well past what its light allows.

How much the grain backs off in the bright parts. At zero it lies evenly over everything, which is what digital noise does; turned up it hides in the midtones and shadows and leaves a blown sky clean, which is what film grain does.

What colour the glow around a highlight takes. On film this is halation rather than bloom — light passes through the emulsion, bounces off the base behind it and exposes the film a second time, and the layer that stops that works least on red. It is why every bulb on a negative wears an orange ring.

What the corners darken toward. Black is the digital answer; a lens simply passing less light at the edge of its circle darkens toward the colour of the light still getting through, which on warm film stock is a brown.

Darkens in a circle instead of following the frame. A single moulded lens element has a round image circle and falls off in a circle regardless of how the picture is cropped out of it; a corrected lens over a rectangular sensor falls off with the rectangle.

The colour the dark half of the picture leans toward. Warming one end of the range and cooling the other is what makes a film stock as opposed to a colour filter — a negative puts teal in the shade, an instant print puts green there.
The colour the bright half leans toward. Gold on a consumer negative, pink on an instant print.
Where the picture is divided between the two tones. Negative hands more of the frame to the shadow colour, positive to the highlight colour.

Raises the black point, so the darkest thing in the picture is a dark grey rather than black. This is the single strongest thing a film look has: a machine print has no true black in it at all, and an instant print has less than any of them.

Tints whatever the lens has actually resolved, so focus can be judged on a preview this small. Viewfinder only — the overlay is drawn into a texture of its own and never reaches a photo, a recording or a stream.
Which colour resolved detail is painted.
The default, and the colour least likely to be mistaken for part of a face or a skin tone.
Reads clearly against red and orange subjects, where red peaks disappear.
For warm, sunlit scenes with no cool colour of their own.
The brightest of the set, for a dark subject where the other colours are hard to pick out.
Neutral, for a saturated scene that fights every coloured overlay.
How readily detail counts as resolved. Higher paints more of the frame; past a point film grain and noise start to peak too.
Drains the colour out of everything but the peaks while peaking is on, which is what makes them unmistakable. The shot itself is unaffected.

Draws framing lines over the viewfinder, so a level horizon and an off-centre subject can be judged rather than guessed. Viewfinder only — the lines are drawn into a texture of their own and never reach a photo, a recording or a stream.
The default. Two lines each way; a subject placed on an intersection reads better than one sat in the middle.
Three lines each way, so the frame has a centre line as well as the off-centre pair.
The placement the rule of thirds rounds off — the same idea, with the lines slightly nearer the middle.
Corner to corner both ways, for lining a shot up along a road, a rail or a leading edge.
One line each way through the middle, for centring a subject and nothing else.
How strongly the lines are drawn over the picture. Each carries a dark edge, so they stay readable against a bright sky as well as a dark subject.

Meters the picture and sets the exposure itself, so a walk from a dark room into daylight stays watchable. The Exposure control above keeps working and becomes compensation on top of what the meter decides.
Which part of the frame the meter listens to.
The whole frame, weighted evenly. The steadiest of the three, and the least likely to swing as things move through the shot.
The whole frame, but the middle counts for far more — the usual stills-camera meter, and the best default for filming a person.
Only a small circle at the centre, so a subject stays exposed against any background. Swings hard when the centre of the frame changes.
How bright the metered part of the picture is driven to. Raise it for a brighter, flatter look; lower it to protect highlights.
How quickly the exposure catches up. Low is a slow, cinematic drift; high reacts at once but can visibly hunt, since the meter is always reading a frame that has already been shown.
Furthest the meter may move the exposure on its own, in stops either way. Keeps a very dark room from being lifted into noise.
Also show the exposure slider on the camera's own interface.
Zooms the image to cover the corners the distortion pulled in. Above 1 crops in, below 1 lets the edges show.
How far the glow spreads out from a highlight, as opposed to how bright it is. Higher is softer and wider.
How far the darkening reaches in from the corners. Low is a hard circle, high fades across most of the frame.
Straightens the stretch a wide lens puts on anything near the edge of frame, the way a panorama is unwrapped. Zero is an ordinary shot.

Darken the creases and contact points on avatars, so a hand resting on an arm reads as touching it rather than floating over it. This only looks at avatars, local and remote - the world around them is not traced, which is what keeps it affordable. Costs real frame time, so it is off by default.

Darken the creases and contact points where surfaces meet. This device has no hardware ray tracing available - on Windows that needs Direct3D12, and Direct3D11 has no ray tracing path at all - so this falls back to a screen space approximation. That version only sees what is already on screen, so every visible surface casts occlusion including the world around you, and the avatars-only setting cannot be applied. Costs real frame time, so it is off by default.

Auto traces the real scene on a graphics card that supports ray tracing and drops to the screen space estimator on one that does not. Ray Traced turns the effect off rather than falling back. Screen Space only sees what is already drawn on screen, but it runs anywhere.
How many rays each pixel casts and how hard the result is filtered afterwards. Higher settles faster and holds more detail; lower leans on the temporal filter and costs less.
How dark the occluded areas on an avatar get. This is a look choice and costs nothing.

How far a surface looks for things that shade it, in metres. At this scale it is contact shadows: the darkening where a hand meets an arm or a strap meets a shoulder. Larger values reach further along a limb and cost more. Only avatars are traced, so nothing in the world casts occlusion.

Lighting feeds the occlusion into how surfaces are lit. It is the truthful option, but it only reaches materials that know how to read it, an avatar's own baked shading can override it, and light coming straight from the sun is barely touched. Final Image darkens the finished picture instead, the way Unity's own ambient occlusion does: it lands on everything, at the cost of dimming light that already has shadows of its own.

How hard the occlusion is smoothed after it is traced. Each step widens the filter without blurring across edges, trading a little contact shadow detail for a cleaner, less grainy result. Turn it up if the shading looks speckled, down if corners look washed out.

Occlusion always dims bounced and ambient light in full. This is how much of it also dims light coming straight from a lamp or the sun. At zero, a brightly lit surface barely changes even where the occlusion buffer looks dark; turning it up brings the shaded image closer to what the buffer shows, at the cost of some realism.

Draw the ambient occlusion on its own instead of through the lighting, so it is obvious what the effect is producing. The shaded image will always show less than this, because occlusion only dims part of the light reaching a surface.

Which buffer Show Occlusion Buffer draws. The occlusion passes through several stages before it reaches the picture, and a fault looks the same in the finished image whichever stage caused it. Step through these and find the first one that shows the problem: that is where it comes from. Final is the composited result, Raw is straight out of the tracer, Temporal is after blending with the previous frame, Denoised is after the blur, and Position and Normal are the surface data everything else is built on.

How many avatars may have their pose handed to the ray tracer in a single frame. Each one is a skin on the processor plus a rebuild of that avatar's geometry, so this is the most expensive thing the occlusion quality buys. Zero follows the quality setting: 1 on Low, 4 on Medium, 16 on High, 100 on Ultra. Any other value pins it, which is how you measure what a busy instance really costs.

Whether mirrors and the handheld camera get their own ambient occlusion. On, a mirror shows the room the same way you see it and photos match the view. Off, only your own view is traced, which is the first thing to turn off when the frame gets tight since every extra camera costs its own pass.
Whether the people in the room darken the surfaces they stand near. Dynamic re-poses them for the trace on a per frame budget, which is processor time the effect does not otherwise spend.
Bounce light from everything on screen, avatars included, onto everything else. Expensive, especially in VR, so it is off by default. When off, worlds cannot switch it on for you.

Screen Space bounces light using what the camera already drew, so anything off screen or behind you contributes nothing. Ray Traced traces the world itself and shades what it hits with the real lights and glowing materials, which costs more and needs a graphics card with ray tracing - without one it falls back to Screen Space.

Whether avatars bounce and block light in the ray traced mode. Dynamic follows them as they move and is the most expensive; Static places them once where they were found; Off leaves people out of the bounce entirely.
How many rays each pixel casts and how far each one is followed. Higher is cleaner and slower; the temporal filter makes up much of the difference while you stand still.
Resolution the bounce is traced at. Bounce light is soft, so Half looks near identical to Full for a quarter of the cost. Photos are always taken at Full.
How much bounced light is added. 1 is the physically motivated amount; higher exaggerates the effect.
How much colour the bounce carries from the surface it came off. Lower it if coloured walls tint the room more than you want.
Ambient occlusion gathered from the same rays as the bounce, so it costs nothing extra. Darkens creases and contact points.
How far, in metres, a ray looks for something to bounce off. Longer picks up light from across a room and costs more per ray.
Width of the edge-aware blur applied to the bounce. Higher hides more of the sampling pattern and softens detail.
A second, wider blur pass. Removes the low frequency blotching a small blur leaves behind, for one more pass over the traced buffer.
Accumulate the bounce across frames. Much cleaner while you stand still; turn it off if you would rather have noise than any trailing.
How much of each new frame replaces the accumulated bounce. Low is the stillest image and trails furthest behind movement; high reacts immediately and is noisier.
Where a ray that hits nothing takes its light from. The reflection probe matches the room; the sky is cheaper and flatter.
Let a ray that leaves the screen keep the light it found at the edge instead of falling back outright. Steadies the bounce near screen borders as you turn.
Carry light from registered emitters analytically. A sign or a strip light is smaller than one traced pixel, and anything behind you is off screen, so neither reaches the bounce any other way.
How much light registered emitters contribute.
Compute the bounce inside reflection probe captures too. A realtime probe pays for the whole effect once per face, so this is off by default.

Which graphics API Basis renders with. DirectX 12 spreads rendering work over more CPU threads, and hardware ray tracing and variable rate shading need it; DirectX 11 is the default and has no first-draw pipeline stalls. Avatars and worlds work on either without rebuilding, since both use the same compiled shaders. The API is chosen as Basis launches, so a change applies on restart, and Basis stays on the one that works if the chosen API is unavailable on this machine.
